attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, stated as his analysis.

semantics.note: Keeps 'most or all of the errors seen thus far' and 'virtually every bit'. Firm assertion about the original Sora's observed errors and its lack of global comprehension.

contract.note: The reading of 'global comprehension' as scene-wide representation of identities and counts follows his examples. Requiring evidence on internal representations is fair, since 'any' is a strong absence claim.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own launch disclosure reports some 3D consistency and object permanence 'often, though not always'. It is a company self-description and not a study of internal representations, so it settles neither side.

reviews.rationale: The only item is OpenAI's account of its own work. It describes partial scene consistency but gives no systematic examination of the faulty clips and no study of internal representations. The packet does not establish that representations were absent, and it does not refute the claim either.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: Narrowed correctly to the chess example. 'Despite ample evidence' is part of the claim and is kept.

contract.note: Context ties 'ample evidence' to training data ('tons of 8x8 boards in the databases'), so asking for evidence of training exposure is a fair, ordinary reading. 'Apprehend' is read as behaviour, which is reasonable.

evidence.note: FIDE rules set the 8x8 standard to check against. They say nothing about Sora's output or its training.
Contemporaneous report that OpenAI did not disclose its training sources. This confirms the gap but does not show how much chess data Sora saw.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in this packet verifies the defective chess output, and no disclosure or audit shows how much chess material Sora was trained on. Neither part of the support condition is established, and nothing contradicts the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A firm, if loose, assertion about the launch-era Sora. In context it rests on the depiction of the monkey-and-chess scene.

contract.note: Reading 'pretty clueless' as failure at elementary chess depiction follows the surrounding example and is an ordinary reading, not a stretched one. The contract also limits it to launch-era behaviour.

evidence.note: A news report quotes a named investor saying the monkey-chess video shows a 7x7 board with three kings. The frames were not recounted, and the March report could draw on earlier commentary.

reviews.rationale: The contract counts a named expert's reported inspection as support, provided its limits are disclosed. The report describes basic structural errors (a 7x7 board, three kings) in the launch-era demonstration, and nothing in the packet contradicts it. Limitation: the frames were not independently inspected, and there is no representative test.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: A sufficiency claim: video-text training did not stop the malformed chess output. 'Impossible outputs like' adds a little, but it matches his 'utterly impossible in chess' in context.

contract.note: The limited sufficiency reading matches his words. The claim needs only video-text training plus the existence of the defective output.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own technical description says captions were generated for all training videos, which establishes the video-text grounding. It is a company disclosure, but it is adequate for a training method.
A news report quotes a named expert describing the 7x7 board with three kings in the Sora monkey-chess video. The board was not independently recounted.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI's disclosure shows Sora was trained on captioned videos, and reputable reporting identifies the 7x7 board with three kings in its output. So that grounding did not prevent the defect. Nothing in the packet disputes the output or where it came from. Limitation: the frames were not inspected directly.
